subject: science
chapter_title: The Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions

concepts.title: Solute, Solvent and Solution
concepts.definition: When salt disappears in water, salt is the solute, water the solvent and the clear uniform mixture the solution; the solute's particles spread between solvent particles so nothing settles on standing and the composition stays the same throughout.
concepts.key_idea: Solute + solvent = solution: one uniform blend with no settling.
concepts.textbook_ref: hecu109.txt lines 46-88 (what are solute, solvent and solution)
question_patterns: define solute, solvent and solution with an example

solution_steps.explain: The dissolved substance is the solute; the dissolving medium is the solvent.
A true solution shows the same taste and composition in every drop.
No settling on standing confirms the solution nature.

concepts.title: Solubility and Saturated Solutions
concepts.definition: Water dissolves only a limiting amount of a solute at a given temperature: while more can still dissolve the solution is unsaturated, but once extra solute settles at the bottom it is saturated, and that maximum amount fixes the solubility of the substance.
concepts.key_idea: Saturation is the dissolving limit at one temperature - heat usually raises the limit.
concepts.textbook_ref: hecu109.txt lines 88-140 (how much solute can dissolve, saturation)
question_patterns: what is a saturated solution - how is it prepared
define solubility of a substance

does solubility depend on temperature - explain with an activity

solution_steps.action: add solute till no more dissolves
solution_steps.explain: Keep stirring in spoonfuls; the first undissolved settling marks saturation.
The limit holds only at that temperature - solubility is temperature-specific.
Heating raises the limit and the settled solute disappears again.

concepts.title: Concentration of a Solution
concepts.definition: Concentration tells how much solute sits in a fixed quantity of solution or solvent; a spoon of salt in 100 mL is dilute while the same spoon in 50 mL is concentrated, and comparing solute-per-solvent ratios settles which of two solutions is stronger.
concepts.key_idea: Count solute per fixed solvent: 4 spoons in 50 mL beats 2 spoons in 100 mL.
question_patterns: which is more concentrated: 2 spoons of salt in 100 mL or 4 spoons in 50 mL

solution_steps.explain: The ratio of dissolved amount to liquid amount measures strength.
Multiplying by 100 compares the solutions per 100 mL of solvent.

concepts.title: Solubility of Gases in Water
concepts.definition: Gases also dissolve in water - oxygen keeps fish alive and the fizz in cold drinks is dissolved carbon dioxide - but gas solubility falls as temperature rises, which is why warm water loses its fizz and boiled water tastes flat.
concepts.key_idea: Cold water holds more gas: heating drives dissolved gases out.
question_patterns: why do aquatic animals survive under water
what is the fizz in cold drinks made of
how does temperature affect the solubility of gases
why does a warm soft drink go flat quickly

compare the solubility of solids and gases on heating

solution_steps.explain: Oxygen and carbon dioxide dissolve in water, supporting life and fizz.
Warming gives gas particles energy to escape, lowering solubility.
Solids usually dissolve more on heating, gases dissolve less.

concepts.title: Density: Mass per Unit Volume
concepts.definition: Density tells how tightly mass is packed in a volume - the crowded bus picture - and is computed as mass divided by volume; it decides whether a substance floats or sinks in water and changes slightly with temperature and pressure.
concepts.key_idea: Divide mass by volume: iron crowds more mass into each cubic centimetre than wood.
concepts.textbook_ref: hecu109.txt lines 297-360 (what is density, formula, dependence)
question_patterns: define density and write its formula

solution_steps.explain: Mass packed per unit volume is the density.

concepts.title: Floating, Sinking and Relative Density
concepts.definition: An object floats in water when its density is less than that of water and sinks when it is more; comparing a substance's density with the density of water gives the relative density that predicts float or sink without trial.
concepts.key_idea: Compare with water: less dense floats, more dense sinks.
concepts.textbook_ref: hecu109.txt lines 280-297 (why objects float or sink), 355-360 (relative density)
question_patterns: why does an iron nail sink but a cork float
define relative density of a substance

calculate the relative density from given densities

solution_steps.explain: Divide the substance density by the density of water.
